name: ETF Garman-Klass range-volatility target: each of 25 ETFs capped to 12% annual volatility, weekly
rule: Portfolio mode rank(universe,t,ctx), long-only. For symbol s: b = universe[s], L = b.length, e = L-1 (the rebalance-day close), r(k) = b[k].close/b[k-1].close - 1; sample std uses n-1. A symbol is scored only if L >= params.need; N = number of scored symbols; if N = 0 return {}. Output weight of s = x_s/N where x_s in [0,1] is its exposure; the remainder is cash (weights sum <= 1). For k=e-20..e: gk_k = 0.5*ln(H_k/L_k)^2 - (2*ln2-1)*ln(C_k/O_k)^2 using that bar's high, low, open, close. sigma = sqrt(mean(gk_k)*252); if mean(gk_k) <= 0 then x_s = 1. Otherwise x_s = min(1, 0.12/sigma). Bonds and gold are usually below 12% and stay fully invested; equity, oil and gas ETFs get cut when their intraday ranges widen.
rationale: A range-based estimator reacts to an intraday blow-out the same day, which close-to-close estimators miss; this tests whether the faster volatility read improves a per-asset volatility cap across a mixed-asset ETF set.
source: Garman & Klass (1980) 'On the Estimation of Security Price Volatilities from Historical Data', Journal of Business 53(1); Moreira & Muir (2017) Journal of Finance 72(4)

name: Downside-risk target: each large cap sized to 15% annual downside deviation (63 days), weekly
rule: Portfolio mode rank(universe,t,ctx), long-only. For symbol s: b = universe[s], L = b.length, e = L-1 (the rebalance-day close), r(k) = b[k].close/b[k-1].close - 1; sample std uses n-1. A symbol is scored only if L >= params.need; N = number of scored symbols; if N = 0 return {}. Output weight of s = x_s/N where x_s in [0,1] is its exposure; the remainder is cash (weights sum <= 1). dd2 = mean over the last 63 returns r(e-62..e) of min(r,0)^2 (threshold 0, all 63 observations in the denominator); dsd = sqrt(dd2*252). If dsd = 0 then x_s = 1 else x_s = min(1, 0.15/dsd).
rationale: Wang-Yan find that scaling by downside risk instead of total variance keeps the up-vol that investors want; this tests that on single large caps where up-vol and down-vol differ a lot (NVDA, TSLA).
source: Wang & Yan (2021) 'Downside risk and the performance of volatility-managed portfolios', Journal of Banking & Finance 131; Moreira & Muir (2017) JF 72(4)

name: Own down-shock stand-down: a large cap that falls more than 3 sigma in a day is held at zero for the next 5 bars
rule: Portfolio mode rank(universe,t,ctx), long-only. For symbol s: b = universe[s], L = b.length, e = L-1 (the rebalance-day close), r(k) = b[k].close/b[k-1].close - 1; sample std uses n-1. A symbol is scored only if L >= params.need; N = number of scored symbols; if N = 0 return {}. Output weight of s = x_s/N where x_s in [0,1] is its exposure; the remainder is cash (weights sum <= 1). For each k in e-4..e (the 5 most recent bars including today): sig_k = sample std of r(k-63..k-1) (the 63 returns ending the bar BEFORE k); shock_k = r(k) < -3*sig_k. x_s = 0 if any shock_k is true else 1.
rationale: Volatility clusters, so a 3-sigma drop tends to be followed by more large moves; this asks if a short own-name stand-down avoids the clustered losses or just misses the rebound.
source: Engle (1982) ARCH, Econometrica 50(4); Schwert (1989) 'Why does stock market volatility change over time?', Journal of Finance 44(5)

name: Crypto volatility-expansion brake: a coin goes to cash while its 10-day volatility is more than twice its 60-day volatility
rule: Portfolio mode rank(universe,t,ctx), long-only. For symbol s: b = universe[s], L = b.length, e = L-1 (the rebalance-day close), r(k) = b[k].close/b[k-1].close - 1; sample std uses n-1. A symbol is scored only if L >= params.need; N = number of scored symbols; if N = 0 return {}. Output weight of s = x_s/N where x_s in [0,1] is its exposure; the remainder is cash (weights sum <= 1). sig10 = sample std of r(e-9..e); sig60 = sample std of r(e-59..e). If sig60 = 0 then x_s = 1. x_s = 0 if sig10 > 2.0*sig60, else 1.
rationale: A sudden multiple of normal volatility marks both crashes and blow-off pumps; stepping out only while the expansion lasts is a cheaper regime filter than a slow moving average, and the test shows whether the exit costs more in missed pumps than it saves.
source: Engle (1982) Econometrica 50(4); Bollerslev (1986) 'Generalized autoregressive conditional heteroskedasticity', Journal of Econometrics 31(3)

name: Bitcoin crash brake: all coins to cash for 14 days after BTC falls 15% over 7 days
rule: Portfolio mode rank(universe,t,ctx), long-only. For symbol s: b = universe[s], L = b.length, e = L-1 (the rebalance-day close), r(k) = b[k].close/b[k-1].close - 1; sample std uses n-1. A symbol is scored only if L >= params.need; N = number of scored symbols; if N = 0 return {}. Output weight of s = x_s/N where x_s in [0,1] is its exposure; the remainder is cash (weights sum <= 1). Let a = universe['BTCUSDT'] (if it is absent return {}); ba = a.length-1 (equal to e for any symbol traded today). A crash day is a bar k with a[k].close/a[k-7].close - 1 <= -0.15. If any crash day exists among the 14 most recent BTC bars (k = ba-13..ba, need ba >= 20) then x_s = 0 for every coin, else x_s = 1 for every scored coin.
rationale: Alt coins fall together with BTC in a crash and recover later; a market-level stand-down is the simplest circuit breaker traders use. With about a dozen distinct episodes the test is blunt, but it asks the exact question people ask.
source: Ji, Bouri, Lau & Roubaud (2019) 'Dynamic connectedness and integration in cryptocurrency markets', International Review of Financial Analysis 63; Diebold & Yilmaz (2012) International Journal of Forecasting 28(1)

name: Reversal-bar stand-down: an ETF goes to cash for 3 bars after a wide-range bar that closes at its low
rule: Portfolio mode rank(universe,t,ctx), long-only. For symbol s: b = universe[s], L = b.length, e = L-1 (the rebalance-day close), r(k) = b[k].close/b[k-1].close - 1; sample std uses n-1. A symbol is scored only if L >= params.need; N = number of scored symbols; if N = 0 return {}. Output weight of s = x_s/N where x_s in [0,1] is its exposure; the remainder is cash (weights sum <= 1). For k in e-2..e (today and the 2 bars before): tr(j) = max(H_j-L_j, |H_j-C_{j-1}|, |L_j-C_{j-1}|); atr_k = simple mean of tr(k-20..k-1) (the 20 bars BEFORE k). Bar k is a flush bar if (H_k-L_k) > 2.0*atr_k AND C_k <= L_k + 0.2*(H_k-L_k) AND C_k < C_{k-1}. x_s = 0 if any k in e-2..e is a flush bar, else 1.
rationale: A big range that closes on its low is the textbook capitulation or distribution bar; the rule tests whether following it with a short stand-down avoids the next leg down or just sells the low before the bounce.
source: Murphy (1999) Technical Analysis of the Financial Markets (key reversal / wide-range bars); Bulkowski (2005) Encyclopedia of Chart Patterns, 2nd ed.

name: Hourly crypto volatility-expansion gate: flat while 24-hour volatility exceeds 1.75x the 30-day hourly volatility
rule: Signal mode signal(bars,i,ctx), long-only, per asset (ctx.state is per asset). Return 0 for every bar until the warm-up is satisfied and whenever a helper returns NaN. Warm-up: i >= 721. s24 = ctx.rollingStd('ret',24,i); s720 = ctx.rollingStd('ret',720,i). If s720 = 0 return 1. Return 0 if s24 > 1.75*s720, else 1 (long).
rationale: Intraday volatility regimes shift fast in crypto; an hourly gate acts on the same clustering as the daily rule but with far more observations, so it tests whether the effect survives at high frequency after costs.
source: Andersen, Bollerslev, Diebold & Labys (2003) 'Modeling and forecasting realized volatility', Econometrica 71(2); Engle (1982) Econometrica 50(4)

name: Crypto correlation-spike halving: cut every coin to half weight when the 30-day average pairwise correlation exceeds 0.70
rule: Portfolio mode rank(universe,t,ctx), long-only. For symbol s: b = universe[s], L = b.length, e = L-1 (the rebalance-day close), r(k) = b[k].close/b[k-1].close - 1; sample std uses n-1. A symbol is scored only if L >= params.need; N = number of scored symbols; if N = 0 return {}. Output weight of s = x_s/N where x_s in [0,1] is its exposure; the remainder is cash (weights sum <= 1). If N < 6 return equal weight 1/N each. Otherwise over the last 30 returns r(e-29..e) compute the Pearson correlation for every pair of scored coins; avgCorr = mean of all pairwise values. m = 0.5 if avgCorr > 0.70 else 1.0; x_s = m for every scored coin.
rationale: When all coins move as one, diversification disappears and a crash hits the whole basket; a correlation-based halving is the crypto version of an absorption-ratio warning light.
source: Kritzman, Li, Page & Rigobon (2011) 'Principal components as a measure of systemic risk', Journal of Portfolio Management 37(4); Longin & Solnik (2001) 'Extreme correlation of international equity markets', Journal of Finance 56(2)

name: Grossman-Zhou drawdown control on 25 ETFs: exposure = 1 - drawdown/20% from the 252-day closing high, weekly
rule: Portfolio mode rank(universe,t,ctx), long-only. For symbol s: b = universe[s], L = b.length, e = L-1 (the rebalance-day close), r(k) = b[k].close/b[k-1].close - 1; sample std uses n-1. A symbol is scored only if L >= params.need; N = number of scored symbols; if N = 0 return {}. Output weight of s = x_s/N where x_s in [0,1] is its exposure; the remainder is cash (weights sum <= 1). peak = max of b[k].close for k = e-251..e; dd = 1 - b[e].close/peak; x_s = max(0, 1 - dd/0.20). A 5% drawdown holds 75%, 10% holds 50%, 20% or worse holds 0. Overseer fix: meta.warmup = 257 (days of the universe calendar), so the deterministic cash warm-up is scored for neither the rule nor B&H.
rationale: Grossman-Zhou's optimal drawdown control scales exposure linearly with the cushion above a floor; it is the textbook continuous drawdown brake and has not been run on a broad ETF set.
source: Grossman & Zhou (1993) 'Optimal investment strategies for controlling drawdowns', Mathematical Finance 3(3)

name: Grossman-Zhou drawdown control on 18 crypto coins: exposure = 1 - drawdown/60% from the 365-day closing high, weekly
rule: Portfolio mode rank(universe,t,ctx), long-only. For symbol s: b = universe[s], L = b.length, e = L-1 (the rebalance-day close), r(k) = b[k].close/b[k-1].close - 1; sample std uses n-1. A symbol is scored only if L >= params.need; N = number of scored symbols; if N = 0 return {}. Output weight of s = x_s/N where x_s in [0,1] is its exposure; the remainder is cash (weights sum <= 1). peak = max of b[k].close for k = e-364..e; dd = 1 - b[e].close/peak; x_s = max(0, 1 - dd/0.60). A 30% drawdown holds 50%, 60% or worse holds 0. Overseer fix: meta.warmup = 370 (days of the universe calendar), so the deterministic cash warm-up is scored for neither the rule nor B&H.
rationale: Crypto drawdowns of 50-80% are routine, so the floor is set at 60%; the question is whether scaling out gradually in a bear market improves risk-adjusted return without the all-or-nothing whipsaw of a stop.
source: Grossman & Zhou (1993) Mathematical Finance 3(3)

name: 52-week-high proximity gate: hold a large cap only while it closes within 15% of its 252-day closing high, weekly
rule: Portfolio mode rank(universe,t,ctx), long-only. For symbol s: b = universe[s], L = b.length, e = L-1 (the rebalance-day close), r(k) = b[k].close/b[k-1].close - 1; sample std uses n-1. A symbol is scored only if L >= params.need; N = number of scored symbols; if N = 0 return {}. Output weight of s = x_s/N where x_s in [0,1] is its exposure; the remainder is cash (weights sum <= 1). peak = max of b[k].close for k = e-251..e; x_s = 1 if b[e].close >= 0.85*peak else 0. Overseer fix: meta.warmup = 257 (days of the universe calendar), so the deterministic cash warm-up is scored for neither the rule nor B&H.
rationale: George-Hwang found stocks near their 52-week high keep outperforming those far below it; used here as an exit rule it removes names in deep drawdown from an equal-weight book and tests the effect on risk rather than selection.
source: George & Hwang (2004) 'The 52-week high and momentum investing', Journal of Finance 59(5)

name: Faber 10-month rule on single large caps: hold a stock only while it closes above its 210-day average, monthly
rule: Portfolio mode rank(universe,t,ctx), long-only. For symbol s: b = universe[s], L = b.length, e = L-1 (the rebalance-day close), r(k) = b[k].close/b[k-1].close - 1; sample std uses n-1. A symbol is scored only if L >= params.need; N = number of scored symbols; if N = 0 return {}. Output weight of s = x_s/N where x_s in [0,1] is its exposure; the remainder is cash (weights sum <= 1). sma = mean of b[k].close for k = e-209..e; x_s = 1 if b[e].close > sma else 0. Overseer fix: meta.warmup = 231 (days of the universe calendar), so the deterministic cash warm-up is scored for neither the rule nor B&H.
rationale: Faber's 10-month rule is proven on asset-class index funds; on single stocks the same rule cuts idiosyncratic drawdowns but whipsaws, and the test measures which wins after costs on today's large caps.
source: Faber (2007) 'A quantitative approach to tactical asset allocation', Journal of Wealth Management 9(4)

name: ATR-band trend filter with hysteresis on 25 ETFs: in above SMA100 + 1 ATR, out below SMA100 - 1 ATR
rule: Signal mode signal(bars,i,ctx), long-only, per asset (ctx.state is per asset). Return 0 for every bar until the warm-up is satisfied and whenever a helper returns NaN. Warm-up i >= 120. m = ctx.sma('close',100,i); a = ctx.atr(20,i). State ctx.state.on starts 0 (flat). If on = 0 and close_i > m + 1.0*a then on = 1. If on = 1 and close_i < m - 1.0*a then on = 0. Return on.
rationale: A fixed-percentage band ignores that a calm bond ETF and a volatile energy ETF have very different noise; scaling the band by ATR is the standard Keltner-style fix for whipsaw and has not been tested.
source: Brock, Lakonishok & LeBaron (1992) 'Simple technical trading rules and the stochastic properties of stock returns', Journal of Finance 47(5); Keltner (1960) How to Make Money in Commodities

name: Kaufman efficiency-ratio trend filter on crypto: hold a coin only if it is above its 100-day average and its 30-day efficiency ratio is at least 0.20
rule: Signal mode signal(bars,i,ctx), long-only, per asset (ctx.state is per asset). Return 0 for every bar until the warm-up is satisfied and whenever a helper returns NaN. Warm-up i >= 100. m = ctx.sma('close',100,i). num = |close_i - close_{i-30}|; den = sum over k=i-29..i of |close_k - close_{k-1}|; ER = den>0 ? num/den : 0. Return 1 if close_i > m AND ER >= 0.20, else 0.
rationale: Moving-average filters bleed in choppy sideways markets; Kaufman's efficiency ratio measures how directional the last 30 days were, so requiring it should skip chop while staying in clean trends.
source: Kaufman (1995) Smarter Trading, McGraw-Hill (efficiency ratio); Kaufman (2013) Trading Systems and Methods, 5th ed.

name: Prior-month-low trailing exit on 25 ETFs: out when the close breaks last month's low, back in on a close above last month's high
rule: Signal mode signal(bars,i,ctx), long-only, per asset (ctx.state is per asset). Return 0 for every bar until the warm-up is satisfied and whenever a helper returns NaN. m = ctx.resample(bars,'1M'); P = the most recent element with complete = true (the previous completed calendar month); warm-up: at least 4 completed months. State ctx.state.on starts 0. If on = 1 and close_i < P.low then on = 0. If on = 0 and close_i > P.high then on = 1. Return on.
rationale: A channel on prior-month extremes is the slow cousin of the Donchian rule that managed-futures funds use; it is a classic mechanical swing stop that only needs two numbers a day and has no tuning parameter.
source: Lukac, Brorsen & Irwin (1988) 'A test of futures market disequilibrium using twelve different technical trading systems', Applied Economics 20; Covel (2009) The Complete TurtleTrader

name: Quarterly loss limit with reset: an ETF is cut to zero for the rest of a quarter once it closes 10% below the prior quarter-end close
rule: Portfolio mode rank(universe,t,ctx), long-only. For symbol s: b = universe[s], L = b.length, e = L-1 (the rebalance-day close), r(k) = b[k].close/b[k-1].close - 1; sample std uses n-1. A symbol is scored only if L >= params.need; N = number of scored symbols; if N = 0 return {}. Output weight of s = x_s/N where x_s in [0,1] is its exposure; the remainder is cash (weights sum <= 1). Quarter of a bar = floor(UTC month/3) of bar.time with the year. Let j be the latest bar index <= e whose quarter differs from the quarter of bar e (the last bar of the previous quarter); if none exists skip s (not scored). q0 = b[j].close; mn = min of b[k].close for k = j+1..e. x_s = 0 if mn < 0.90*q0, else 1. The stop therefore resets at the first bar of each new quarter.
rationale: Fund managers run period loss limits that reset; Kaminski-Lo show a stop with a re-entry rule only helps under momentum. A calendar-reset stop avoids picking a re-entry signal, which makes it a clean test of the stop itself.
source: Kaminski & Lo (2014) 'When do stop-loss rules stop losses?', Journal of Financial Markets 18

name: Own-composite trend gate on 40 large caps: hold all 40 only while their equal-weight index is above its 150-day average, daily
rule: Portfolio mode rank(universe,t,ctx), long-only. For symbol s: b = universe[s], L = b.length, e = L-1 (the rebalance-day close), r(k) = b[k].close/b[k-1].close - 1; sample std uses n-1. A symbol is scored only if L >= params.need; N = number of scored symbols; if N = 0 return {}. Output weight of s = x_s/N where x_s in [0,1] is its exposure; the remainder is cash (weights sum <= 1). Build composite levels C_k for k=e-209..e: C_{e-209} = 1; C_k = C_{k-1}*(1 + mean over scored symbols of r_s(k)). m = mean of C_k for k=e-149..e. gate = 1 if C_e > m else 0. x_s = gate for every scored symbol. Overseer fix: meta.warmup = 211 (days of the universe calendar), so the deterministic cash warm-up is scored for neither the rule nor B&H. Overseer fix: rebalance daily instead of weekly (a weekly gate flips only about 29 times on the cached history, under the 30-trade floor; daily about 65).
rationale: A market-level gate costs one decision instead of forty; this tests Faber-style timing on an equal-weight large-cap index built from the universe itself (not the S&P, which is held out).
source: Faber (2007) JWM 9(4); Brock et al. (1992) Journal of Finance 47(5)

name: Crypto blow-off trim: a coin is held at half weight while it is more than 50% above its level 14 days ago
rule: Portfolio mode rank(universe,t,ctx), long-only. For symbol s: b = universe[s], L = b.length, e = L-1 (the rebalance-day close), r(k) = b[k].close/b[k-1].close - 1; sample std uses n-1. A symbol is scored only if L >= params.need; N = number of scored symbols; if N = 0 return {}. Output weight of s = x_s/N where x_s in [0,1] is its exposure; the remainder is cash (weights sum <= 1). ret14 = b[e].close/b[e-14].close - 1. x_s = 0.5 if ret14 > 0.50 else 1.
rationale: Parabolic two-week runs in crypto are followed by reversals; halving through the spike is the lowest-regret way to test it, since it keeps half the upside if the run continues.
source: Liu & Tsyvinski (2021) 'Risks and returns of cryptocurrency', Review of Financial Studies 34(6); Bali, Cakici & Whitelaw (2011) 'Maxing out', Journal of Financial Economics 99(2)

name: ATR extension trim: a large cap is held at half weight while it closes more than 4 ATR above its 50-day average
rule: Portfolio mode rank(universe,t,ctx), long-only. For symbol s: b = universe[s], L = b.length, e = L-1 (the rebalance-day close), r(k) = b[k].close/b[k-1].close - 1; sample std uses n-1. A symbol is scored only if L >= params.need; N = number of scored symbols; if N = 0 return {}. Output weight of s = x_s/N where x_s in [0,1] is its exposure; the remainder is cash (weights sum <= 1). sma50 = mean of b[k].close for k=e-49..e; tr(j) = max(H_j-L_j, |H_j-C_{j-1}|, |L_j-C_{j-1}|); atr = simple mean of tr(e-13..e). x_s = 0.5 if b[e].close > sma50 + 4.0*atr else 1.
rationale: Swing traders sell into climax runs that stretch far above the 50-day line; this tests that rule as a risk trim on large caps, where short-term reversal is a documented effect.
source: Wilder (1978) New Concepts in Technical Trading Systems (ATR); Jegadeesh (1990) 'Evidence of predictable behavior of security returns', Journal of Finance 45(3)

name: Stale-high exit on 25 ETFs: hold an ETF only if its latest 100-day closing high was set within the last 50 bars, weekly
rule: Portfolio mode rank(universe,t,ctx), long-only. For symbol s: b = universe[s], L = b.length, e = L-1 (the rebalance-day close), r(k) = b[k].close/b[k-1].close - 1; sample std uses n-1. A symbol is scored only if L >= params.need; N = number of scored symbols; if N = 0 return {}. Output weight of s = x_s/N where x_s in [0,1] is its exposure; the remainder is cash (weights sum <= 1). Over k = e-99..e find the LATEST bar index kh holding the maximum close; age = e - kh. x_s = 1 if age <= 50 else 0. Overseer fix: meta.warmup = 105 (days of the universe calendar), so the deterministic cash warm-up is scored for neither the rule nor B&H.
rationale: An asset that has not made a new high in half a window is in a range or in decline; time-since-high is a trend-quality read that does not depend on the price level, unlike a moving average.
source: Lo, Mamaysky & Wang (2000) 'Foundations of technical analysis', Journal of Finance 55(4); Murphy (1999) Technical Analysis of the Financial Markets

name: Minervini breakdown exit on large caps: out when a stock closes below its 50-day average on 1.5x volume, back in above the 50-day
rule: Signal mode signal(bars,i,ctx), long-only, per asset (ctx.state is per asset). Return 0 for every bar until the warm-up is satisfied and whenever a helper returns NaN. Warm-up i >= 60. m = ctx.sma('close',50,i); v = ctx.sma('volume',20,i). On the first warm bar set ctx.state.on = (close_i > m ? 1 : 0). Afterwards: if on = 1 and close_i < m and volume_i > 1.5*v then on = 0; if on = 0 and close_i > m then on = 1. Return on.
rationale: O'Neil and Minervini both say a heavy-volume close under the 50-day line is the sell signal and a quiet one is not; this checks whether the volume condition adds anything over the plain moving-average exit.
source: O'Neil (1988) How to Make Money in Stocks; Minervini (2013) Trade Like a Stock Market Wizard

name: Dow higher-low structure on crypto: hold a coin while its 20-bar low is above the low of the 20 bars before
rule: Signal mode signal(bars,i,ctx), long-only, per asset (ctx.state is per asset). Return 0 for every bar until the warm-up is satisfied and whenever a helper returns NaN. Warm-up i >= 40. lowNow = min of bars[k].low for k=i-19..i; lowPrev = min of bars[k].low for k=i-39..i-20. Return 1 if lowNow > lowPrev else 0.
rationale: Dow theory defines an uptrend as a series of higher lows; a rolling-window version needs no moving average and is a swing-structure test that has a long track record in the Brown-Goetzmann-Kumar re-study.
source: Brown, Goetzmann & Kumar (1998) 'The Dow Theory: William Peter Hamilton's track record reconsidered', Journal of Finance 53(4); Rhea (1932) The Dow Theory

name: Fast EMA trend-rider on large caps: out after 2 straight closes below the 21-day EMA, back in when the 10-day EMA is above it and the close is above it
rule: Signal mode signal(bars,i,ctx), long-only, per asset (ctx.state is per asset). Return 0 for every bar until the warm-up is satisfied and whenever a helper returns NaN. Warm-up i >= 40. e21(j) = ctx.ema('close',21,j), e10 = ctx.ema('close',10,i). On the first warm bar ctx.state.on = (close_i > e21(i) ? 1 : 0). Afterwards: if on = 1 and close_i < e21(i) and close_{i-1} < e21(i-1) then on = 0; if on = 0 and e10 > e21(i) and close_i > e21(i) then on = 1. Return on.
rationale: Momentum traders ride a stock until it loses the 21-day EMA; testing that exit as a pure risk overlay on large caps shows whether the short-term trailing exit is worth its trading cost.
source: Han, Yang & Zhou (2013) 'A new anomaly: the cross-sectional profitability of technical analysis', Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis 48(5); Brock et al. (1992) JF 47(5)

name: Monthly MACD trend filter on 25 ETFs: hold while the monthly MACD(12,26,9) is above its signal line
rule: Signal mode signal(bars,i,ctx), long-only, per asset (ctx.state is per asset). Return 0 for every bar until the warm-up is satisfied and whenever a helper returns NaN. m = ctx.resample(bars,'1M'); use only elements with complete = true; need at least 34 completed months else return 0. Over the monthly closes: macd_t = EMA12(c)_t - EMA26(c)_t (each EMA seeded with the SMA of its first n closes); sig_t = EMA9 of macd (seeded with the SMA of its first 9 values); evaluate at the last completed month: return 1 if macd > sig, else 0. The value only changes when a new month completes. Overseer fix: meta.warmup = 720 (bars per asset, about 34 months), so the deterministic cash warm-up is scored for neither the rule nor B&H. Overseer fix: 34 months is the earliest the 9-month signal seed exists (EMA26 seeded at month 26, signal SMA over macd months 26-34), not 40; meta.warmup excludes it from scoring.
rationale: The monthly MACD is a long-standing slow trend filter chartists use for allocation; it has fewer than 10 flips per asset over the sample so costs are tiny, and the test shows whether it avoids the big drawdowns.
source: Appel (2005) Technical Analysis: Power Tools for Active Investors, FT Press; Murphy (1999) Technical Analysis of the Financial Markets

name: Hourly crypto flash-crash brake: flat for 24 hours after a close 8% below the 48-hour closing high
rule: Signal mode signal(bars,i,ctx), long-only, per asset (ctx.state is per asset). Return 0 for every bar until the warm-up is satisfied and whenever a helper returns NaN. Warm-up i >= 80. For k in i-23..i: hi_k = max of bars[j].close for j=k-48..k-1 (the 48 bars BEFORE k); crash_k = close_k <= 0.92*hi_k. Return 0 if any crash_k is true, else 1.
rationale: Liquidation cascades in crypto happen within hours; a 24-hour hourly brake tests whether stepping aside after a flush avoids continued selling or only misses the recovery.
source: Cont (2001) 'Empirical properties of asset returns: stylized facts and statistical issues', Quantitative Finance 1(2); Andersen et al. (2003) Econometrica 71(2)

name: Beta tilt when the market turns: 40 large caps equal weight, but only the 10 lowest-beta names while their composite is below its 200-day average, weekly
rule: Portfolio mode rank(universe,t,ctx), long-only. For symbol s: b = universe[s], L = b.length, e = L-1 (the rebalance-day close), r(k) = b[k].close/b[k-1].close - 1; sample std uses n-1. A symbol is scored only if L >= params.need; N = number of scored symbols; if N = 0 return {}. Output weight of s = x_s/N where x_s in [0,1] is its exposure; the remainder is cash (weights sum <= 1). If N < 20 return equal weight 1/N each. Composite returns rc(k) = mean over scored symbols of r_s(k) for k = e-251..e; levels C_{e-252} = 1, C_k = C_{k-1}*(1+rc(k)). trendUp = C_e > mean of C_k for k=e-199..e. If trendUp: x_s = 1 for every scored symbol. Else: beta_s = cov(r_s, rc)/var(rc) over k=e-251..e; the 10 scored symbols with the lowest beta (ties by symbol name ascending) get weight 0.1 each, all others 0. Overseer fix: meta.warmup = 260 (days of the universe calendar), so the deterministic cash warm-up is scored for neither the rule nor B&H.
rationale: Low-beta stocks lose less in a down market but are not cash; this overlay stays fully invested in defensives while the trend is down, so it tests whether a beta tilt beats raw de-risking.
source: Frazzini & Pedersen (2014) 'Betting against beta', Journal of Financial Economics 111(1); Baker, Bradley & Wurgler (2011) 'Benchmarks as limits to arbitrage', Financial Analysts Journal 67(1)

name: Own-history volatility percentile ladder on 25 ETFs: full below the 75th percentile, half 75th-90th, zero above the 90th, weekly
rule: Portfolio mode rank(universe,t,ctx), long-only. For symbol s: b = universe[s], L = b.length, e = L-1 (the rebalance-day close), r(k) = b[k].close/b[k-1].close - 1; sample std uses n-1. A symbol is scored only if L >= params.need; N = number of scored symbols; if N = 0 return {}. Output weight of s = x_s/N where x_s in [0,1] is its exposure; the remainder is cash (weights sum <= 1). For each k in e-503..e: sig_k = sample std of r(k-20..k). p = fraction of those 504 values with sig_k <= sig_e. x_s = 1 if p < 0.75; 0.5 if 0.75 <= p < 0.90; 0 if p >= 0.90. Overseer fix: meta.warmup = 532 (days of the universe calendar), so the deterministic cash warm-up is scored for neither the rule nor B&H.
rationale: Judging each ETF against its own history means bonds are cut when bond vol is abnormal and equities when equity vol is; a percentile ladder is the common implementation of 'de-risk in high-vol regimes' without a volatility target.
source: Bollerslev, Hood, Huss & Pedersen (2018) 'Risk everywhere: modeling and managing volatility', Review of Financial Studies 31(7); Moreira & Muir (2017) JF 72(4)

name: MAX-effect trim: a large cap is held at half weight for as long as its largest daily gain in the last 21 days exceeds 7%, weekly
rule: Portfolio mode rank(universe,t,ctx), long-only. For symbol s: b = universe[s], L = b.length, e = L-1 (the rebalance-day close), r(k) = b[k].close/b[k-1].close - 1; sample std uses n-1. A symbol is scored only if L >= params.need; N = number of scored symbols; if N = 0 return {}. Output weight of s = x_s/N where x_s in [0,1] is its exposure; the remainder is cash (weights sum <= 1). mx = max of r(e-20..e). x_s = 0.5 if mx > 0.07 else 1.
rationale: Stocks with a recent lottery-like jump have lower future returns; used as a sizing trim on large caps it tests whether lowering weight after jumps (earnings gaps, news) improves risk without needing a stock-selection rule.
source: Bali, Cakici & Whitelaw (2011) 'Maxing out: stocks as lotteries and the cross-section of expected returns', Journal of Financial Economics 99(2)

name: Trend-persistence exposure on crypto: weight = share of the last 20 days a coin closed above its own 50-day average, weekly
rule: Portfolio mode rank(universe,t,ctx), long-only. For symbol s: b = universe[s], L = b.length, e = L-1 (the rebalance-day close), r(k) = b[k].close/b[k-1].close - 1; sample std uses n-1. A symbol is scored only if L >= params.need; N = number of scored symbols; if N = 0 return {}. Output weight of s = x_s/N where x_s in [0,1] is its exposure; the remainder is cash (weights sum <= 1). For j in e-19..e: above_j = b[j].close > mean of b[k].close for k=j-49..j. x_s = (count of above_j)/20.
rationale: A binary moving-average gate flips on a single day; the share of recent days above the average is a smooth exposure that responds to persistent trends and ignores one-off crossings.
source: Hurst, Ooi & Pedersen (2017) 'A century of evidence on trend-following investing', Journal of Portfolio Management 44(1); Zakamulin (2017) Market Timing with Moving Averages

name: Bitcoin volatility-percentile gate: all coins to cash while BTC's 30-day volatility is in the top quintile of its trailing two years
rule: Portfolio mode rank(universe,t,ctx), long-only. For symbol s: b = universe[s], L = b.length, e = L-1 (the rebalance-day close), r(k) = b[k].close/b[k-1].close - 1; sample std uses n-1. A symbol is scored only if L >= params.need; N = number of scored symbols; if N = 0 return {}. Output weight of s = x_s/N where x_s in [0,1] is its exposure; the remainder is cash (weights sum <= 1). Let a = universe['BTCUSDT'] (absent or fewer than 761 bars: return equal weight 1/N each). ra(k) = a[k].close/a[k-1].close - 1. For k = ba-729..ba (ba = a.length-1): sig_k = sample std of ra(k-29..k). p = fraction of those 730 values with sig_k <= sig_ba. If p >= 0.80 then x_s = 0 for every coin, else 1. Overseer fix: threshold 0.80 instead of 0.90 (a 0.90 gate flips only about 21 times on the cached history, under the 30-trade floor; 0.80 about 41). Chosen from the flip count alone, no return was computed.
rationale: BTC sets the volatility regime for the whole market; a market-level gate on its volatility percentile is a simpler, cheaper rule than 18 per-coin rules and asks whether crypto crises are predictable from volatility alone.
source: Moreira & Muir (2017) JF 72(4); Bollerslev et al. (2018) RFS 31(7); Liu & Tsyvinski (2021) RFS 34(6)
